questions.q: Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined word in the given sentence.
questions.s:
Correct answer:smarter

Explanation:

The sentence is: "Mita is ___ than many other kids in the school."
This sentence involves a comparison between two entities: Mita and other kids.

  • When comparing two things or people, we use the comparative degree of adjectives.

  • The correct comparative form of "smart" is "smarter."

Let’s evaluate the options:

  • Smarter – comparative form of “smart” → ✅ correct

  • Less smart – also comparative, but suggests inferiority, which changes the meaning

  • Most smart – incorrect form; the correct superlative is smartest

  • Smartest – superlative form, used when comparing more than two or showing the highest degree → not suitable here

Hence, smarter is the correct substitution for the underlined word.

questions.q:
From the given options, identify the segment which contains the grammatical error.

The more you (A)/study, the most (B)/you learn. (C)/No error (D)
questions.s:
The error lies in part 'B'.
Key Points

  • The given above sentence is grammatically incorrect. 
  • Use 'the more' in place of 'the most'.
  • As a general rule, in some sentences, comparative degrees are split and used in two parts of the sentence. In such sentences, comparative degree should be used in both parts.
  • Let's have a look at the structural form of given rule:
    • The (more / less) + (noun / noun phrase) subject + verb + , + the (more / less) + (noun) subject + verb.
  • ​Example:
    • The higher a man rises, the humbler he grows. 
    • The higher you go, the cooler you feel. 
  • ​Here, the most(superlative degree) is used in the second part of the sentence that is incorrect.
  • So, as per the given points, the most appropriate option is Option 3.
     

Correct sentence: The more you study, the more you learn.

Mistake Points

  • In such types of given sentences, we can not use comparative in one part and positive or superlative in the other part of the sentence.
  • Example:
    • The higher a man rises, the humble/humblest he grows. 
    • The higher you go, the cool/coolest you feel. 

​​Additional Information

  • As a general rule, when we want to emphasize continuous change, we can use two comparative adjectives separated by and.
  • In such types of sentences, the comparative adjective is repeated one after the other.
  • Example:
    • As Microsoft grew, Bill Gates got richer and richer. 
    • As Microsoft grew, Bill Gates got rich and richer.
